Ecce, habes de principibus Dorothielis ex quolibet ordine diurno scilicet & nocturno 24. duces, cum numero servitorum decem millium centum sexaginta. Et nota, quod operatio per istos multum est à caeteris diversa, quemadmodum largè de domino dicemus. Nam secundum 12. horas diei & noctis operandum est in mansione ista, semperque duabus horis praesunt quatuor principes, tam in die quam in nocte; ita, ut non liceat tibi advocare alium, nisi ex ordine, quem hora concernit; ut si fit operatio in prima vel in secunda hora diei, voca quem volueris, ex primis quatuor, qui praesunt diei, si in tertia vel quarta, ex secundis quatuor ducem noveris esse vocandum. Et ita consequenter est faciendum per omnes ordines & 24. horas tam in die quam in nocte. Cum autem volueris operari in Steganographia per spiritus ipsius Dorothielis praemissis generalibus in arte praemitti consuetis, scribe literas qualescunque volueris, vertensque te ad eam plagam orbis, quam à vento communiter Chorum appellamus, voca unum aut plures ex quatuor, qui praesunt horae, in qua operaris.

Behold, you have from the princes of Dorothiel, from every order (that is, diurnal and nocturnal), 24 dukes, with a number of servants totaling ten thousand one hundred and sixty. And note that the operation through these is quite different from the others, just as we shall speak at length concerning the lord. For one must operate in this mansion according to the 12 hours of the day and the night, and four princes always preside over two hours, as much in the day as in the night; in such a way that it is not permitted for you to call another, except from the order that the hour concerns. If the operation is in the first or second hour of the day, call whichever of the first four presiding over the day you wish; if in the third or fourth, you will know the duke must be called from the second four. And so it must be done consequently through all orders and 24 hours, both in the day and in the night. When, however, you wish to operate in Steganography through the spirits of Dorothiel himself with the general premises accustomed to be placed at the start of the art, write whatever letters you wish, and turning yourself to that region of the orb which we commonly call Chorus by the wind, call one or more from the four who preside over the hour in which you operate.

Qualitas mutata vel in parte, uel in toto conspi-

Itaq, in parte occurrit oculorū lippitudo sicca, (qua-

XXVI.
In toto uerò ariditas & squallor, ut quasi sceleton
uideatur. Quamuis enim concoctio mala fiat & ali-

à cibo luculentior.

XXVII.
Quòd si Hectica cum putrida iungatur, putridæ no-
tas habebit adiunctas.

LXVIII.
Incipientem Hecticam cognoscere difficile, factam
curare arduum, nosse procliuè. *Marasmodes* est imme-
dicabilis, cum fibrosa partis substantia instaurari ne-

translation:
**XXIII.**
But generally, in any *Hectic* [fever], the earwax is dry. Distillations are sharp and salty. Sweats [occur] on almost every night. Feces are generally dry, in some [cases] even liquid.

**XXIV.**
A changed quality is observed either in a part or in the whole.

**XXV.**
Thus, in a part, one encounters dry lippitude <note>inflammation of the eyelids</note> of the eyes (such as [that of] those who have completed a long journey in the sun and dust), concave eyes, collapsed temples, sharp nostrils, rigid ears and eyebrows. The vivid color of the face has perished; finally, the face is *Hippocratic* <note>a pinched, sunken, and pale facial expression indicative of impending death</note>.

**XXVI.**
In the whole, however, [there is] dryness and squalor, so that one appears as if a skeleton. For although digestion is poorly performed and the nourishment is depraved, cachexia <note>general physical wasting</note> does not occur, because it is consumed by the heat and dryness of the limbs: with apologies to Celsus, who seems to have listed cachexia among the species of Hectic. Heat is more distinct after food.

**XXVII.**
But if the Hectic [fever] is joined with a putrid [fever], it will have the signs of the putrid [fever] attached.

**XXVIII.**
To recognize an incipient Hectic [fever] is difficult, to cure one established is arduous, to know [one at its end] is easy. *Marasmodes* is immedicable, since the fibrous substance of the part cannot be restored.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual hierarchy, transitioning from the comparison between angels and humans to a detailed analysis of the tripartite soul (Nephesh, Ruach, and Neshamah) and their origins within the Sephiroth, the divine emanations of Kabbalistic thought.</meta>

three parts, which are <term>Nephesh</term> <note>The lowest of the three parts of the soul.</note>, <term>Ruach</term> <note>The middle soul, associated with the spirit and emotions.</note>, and <term>Neshamah</term> <note>The highest soul, associated with the intellect and divine spark.</note>. The Nephesh is the vehicle of the Ruach, just as the Ruach is the vehicle of the Neshamah. Moreover, the emanation of all three is from the higher <term>Sephiroth</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>, which are the roots of all roots. They differ, however, in their source of emanation; for the Neshamah emanates from <term>Binah</term> <note>Understanding; the third Sephirah.</note>, as indicated in <margin>Job 32:8.</margin> *“And the breath <note>original: "Neschamah"</note> of the Almighty <note>original: "Schadai"</note> gives them understanding.”* The Ruach, however, emanates from <term>Tiphereth</term> <note>Beauty or Compassion; the sixth Sephirah.</note>; and just as Tiphereth is the throne and dwelling place of Binah, so the Ruach is the throne and dwelling place of the Neshamah. But the Nephesh emanates from <term>Malchuth</term> <note>Kingdom; the tenth and lowest Sephirah, associated with the physical realm.</note>, and thus the Nephesh is the throne and dwelling place of the Ruach, just as Malchuth is the throne and dwelling place of Tiphereth.

Rabbi <term>Shimon bar Yochai</term> <note>original: "Schimeon Jochā"; the traditional author of the Zohar.</note> (may his memory be a blessing) explains their emanation in the section *Vayechi* in the <term>Zohar</term> <note>The foundational work of Jewish mysticism.</note>, folio 113, column d, with these words: "Learn, all things consist of steps established one above the other: Nephesh, Ruach, Neshamah, one level higher than the next. The Nephesh is first, which is the lowest level, as stated elsewhere; then the Ruach, which rests upon the Nephesh and has the Neshamah standing above it as the highest level of all, as has been established. This Nephesh is the Nephesh of David (concerning which see 2 Samuel 5:8, regarding Malchuth), to which it is appointed to receive Nephesh from that stream which flows and goes out. The Ruach is established over it, and the Nephesh cannot endure except through the Ruach, that spirit which is placed between Fire and Water (namely Tiphereth, which stands between <term>Gevurah</term> <note>original: "Gebhurah"; Strength/Severity, associated with Fire.</note> and <term>Gedulah</term> <note>Greatness/Mercy, associated with Water.</note>). And by this Ruach, the Nephesh is nourished. The Ruach itself endures through the state of another higher level, which is the Neshamah, from which both the Nephesh and Ruach are sustained. Thus, when the Ruach has participated, the Nephesh then participates, and all are one, and they cling to each other: the Nephesh to the Ruach, and the Ruach to the Neshamah, and all are one." Thus he spoke. The meaning of which is that the Neshamah is Binah, the Ruach is Tiphereth, and the Nephesh is Malchuth.
